result:
The museum of unfinished things opened on a Tuesday because its founder had never managed to finish planning the opening ceremony.

There was no ribbon. A pair of scissors rested on a folding chair beside the entrance, along with a note that read: **Something red, probably.**

Inside, the first exhibit was a sweater.

It had one sleeve and most of another. The yarn was the pale blue of a winter afternoon, and the unfinished cuff trailed down into a basket. According to the card, it had been knitted by a woman who learned halfway through that her grandson preferred green.

She had put it away to begin again. Then spring arrived, followed by other things.

Across from the sweater stood a dining table with three sanded legs and one still rough. Visitors were allowed to touch the rough leg. They did, almost without exception.

The east gallery contained apologies.

Some were written on paper. Others existed only as descriptions supplied by the people who had almost delivered them.

*I’m sorry I made you feel foolish when you were excited.*

*I should have come to the hospital.*

*You were right about the dog.*

This was the quietest room. A bench had been placed near the window. It was finished, but nobody objected.

Upstairs were novels abandoned after eleven pages, gardens overtaken by weeds, a language someone had studied until they could order coffee but not explain why they were sad. There was a violin purchased at forty-seven and played six times. There was a map for a journey whose maker had instead stayed home to care for his father.

The museum had difficulty deciding what to put on the cards.

Some objects had been abandoned. Some had been interrupted. A few had simply become unnecessary, though their owners had kept them for years, reluctant to throw away the evidence of an earlier intention.

The founder began leaving more space beneath each description.

Children loved the room of unfinished drawings. They were invited to add anything they liked, provided they did not try to complete a picture according to its apparent original plan. A horse might acquire a doorway in its side. A house might stand on enormous bird legs. One child carefully added a small moon to every drawing she could reach.

On Thursdays, the museum stayed open late.

People came after work carrying boxes. A man brought a model ship with no sails. A woman brought an application form for music school, dated thirty-two years earlier. Someone brought half a friendship bracelet and declined to explain.

The founder accepted nearly everything.

But one evening, a visitor arrived empty-handed and asked whether an entire life could qualify.

The founder considered this for a while.

Then she fetched another folding chair from the storeroom and set it beside her own.

They sat together until closing time. The visitor helped her turn out the lights.
